newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Pensioners, IMF snap at Kazakh govt's heels.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pensioners, IMF snap at Kazakh govt's heels.

text.p: Kazakhstan's government, under fire from angry pensioners and under pressure from the International Monetary Fund to hold to a tight budget, on Wednesday maintained that it could still please both.

Worried by discontent among a 16.9 million population fed up with huge debts to state employees and pensioners, President Nursultan Nazarbayev has given the government until the end of the year to find the cash.
But while the reformist government has vowed to meet the deadline, it has to find 36 billion tenge ($480 million) it does not have under the tough glare of the IMF.
First Deputy Prime Minister Akhmetzhan Yesimov was sent to Washington to meet senior IMF officials this week to provide explanation after a new law on tax privileges provoked the fund's ire.

International finance sources in Almaty, one of whom described the new tax law as "institutionalised corruption", said the law had seriously theatened Kazakhstan's $446 million Extended Fund Facility agreed with the IMF last year.
The fund's resident representative in Kazakhstan, David Hoelscher, said relations were back on track.
"There is agreement in principle for the 1997 programme which will be discussed at a board meeting in Washington later this month," he said.
But, like Kazakh officials, Hoelscher declined to say what compromise was reached or which side had backed down.

The ex-Soviet state, an area of steppe and mountain the size of western Europe sitting on huge reserves of oil and gas, is looking to a $300 million Eurobond issue and receipts from a rapid-fire privatisation programme to find the money.
But on Wednesday, Deputy Finance Minister Zhanat Yertlesova said the government might increase the budget gap from 3.16 percent of gross domestic product to 4.16 percent.
"The budget deficit was approved (by parliament) at 3.16 percent of GDP but now we might raise it up to 4.16 percent," Yertlesova told a news conference.

She explained that the government was considering increasing the budget gap to 3.66 percent and that if there was still not enough cash for pensioners, then the deficit would be upped to 4.16 percent.
"All these questions have been worked out with the IMF," she said, adding that she expected the Fund to approve a new tranche of the loan at an IMF board meeting in Washington next week.
A western banker who watches Kazakhstan closely but who declined to be named said, "Both sides are trying hard to come to an agreement."
But he said the Kazakhs might lose the three-year extended fund facility and be demoted to a year-long stand-by loan.
Kazakhstan so far has not used any of the existing loan, a sign, said Yertlesova, that market reforms are chugging along "fine".
This month it published its lowest inflation figure since the start of reforms in 1992 -- 0.4 percent for May versus 0.8 percent in April.
But anxious to cement an image as a safe place to do business, the Kazakh government has been careful to keep on the right side of the IMF.
"It's not a precondition to investment but many in the markets look to IMF support for assurance," the banker said.
